subtype: Sports practice fatigue and short temper [Observer]
passage: Shreya, now that you're coaching, let me, Sharmila, tell you about Harpreet. The children called me Sharmila Ma'am. Harpreet was fifteen, always first to warm-up, always laughing. One hot May week she changed. She jogged at the back, dragged her feet in the relays and snapped at a teammate who only asked for the baton. I had a whole speech ready about attitude and effort. Then I saw her bottle lying empty since morning, her face flushed and blotchy. I sat her in the shade with water and let her rest out the next drill. That week I added water breaks between every drill for the whole squad. Harpreet was laughing again by Friday. No pep talk of mine ever did what that water jug did.

qa.q: What did Harpreet snap at a teammate about?
qa.a: The teammate only asked for the baton.

qa.q: What was Sharmila tempted to do, and how did she feel?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and was ready with a speech about attitude and effort, before she noticed the empty bottle.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sharmila's story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Choosing water and rest in the shade over a lecture, then adding water breaks for everyone; it fixed the body's need behind the mood.

qa.q: How might that week have felt for Harpreet?
qa.a: Probably draining and confusing; she was hot and dried out, so running felt heavy and small requests made her snap.

grounding: Shows a coach noticing a usually keen teen turn slow and sharp after training in heat without drinking, and water breaks helping more than a pep talk.

subtype: Sports practice fatigue and short temper [Observer]
passage: The district kho-kho trials were three days away, the heat was brutal, and the ground's tap had run dry. Coach Uday watched Manjula, sixteen and usually the loudest in the team, trudge through her chases. When a teammate tagged her out, she threw her cap and muttered, "What's the point?" Uday felt his temper rise; he had no time for sulks this week. Then he saw her lips, dry and pale, and remembered the empty tap. He blew the whistle, sent two players to the shop with money from his own wallet and made everyone sit in the shade and drink. Manjula drank a whole bottle in silence. After a short rest she was back, laughing at her own clumsy fall.

qa.q: Why was there no water at the ground?
qa.a: The ground's tap had run dry.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when Manjula threw her cap?
qa.a: He felt his temper rise under the pressure of the trials, before he noticed her dry, pale lips.

qa.q: What did Uday choose, and why was it better than a scolding?
qa.a: He stopped practice for water and rest in the shade, which dealt with the heat and thirst behind the mood instead of the mood itself.

qa.q: What was the practice like for Manjula before the break?
qa.a: She was probably exhausted and dried out, so every chase felt pointless and a small loss made her snap.

grounding: Illustrates a coach under time pressure seeing a keen teen turn slow and moody in the heat and choosing water and rest over a pep talk.

subtype: Sports practice fatigue and short temper [Observer]
passage: Dhruv was usually the loudest voice on the basketball court behind the colony school in Chennai, first to every loose ball. Today, forty minutes into drills under a white-hot sky, Coach Harish watched him jog instead of sprint, miss easy layups, and snap "I know!" when a teammate called the play. Harish felt the old urge to blow the whistle and give a speech about attitude. Instead he looked at the sideline. Dhruv's bottle stood there, still sealed. "Water break, everyone. Five minutes, in the shade." He tossed Dhruv the bottle. "All of it." Dhruv drank, sat against the wall, and after five minutes grinned for the first time that afternoon. That night Harish added a water whistle every fifteen minutes to the practice plan.

qa.q: What did Harish notice about Dhruv's bottle?
qa.a: It was still sealed.

qa.q: What was Harish tempted to do, and why did he change his mind?
qa.a: He felt irritated and wanted to lecture about attitude, but grew curious and concerned enough to check the sideline, where he spotted the sealed bottle.

qa.q: Why is Harish's water whistle better than a pep talk?
qa.a: It fixes the physical cause of the slow, sharp mood for the whole team at every practice.

qa.q: What is practice like for Dhruv before the break?
qa.a: He is drained and irritable, slow on his feet and snapping at teammates, not his usual enthusiastic self.

grounding: Shows a coach seeing a keen teen turn slow and sharp after training in heat without water, and choosing a water break over a pep talk.

Coach Chetan blew his whistle. "Neelam! That's the third pass you've dropped."
"I'm trying, Sir!"
"You're dragging your feet. Where's the fire from last week?"
"I don't know. My head hurts and everyone's annoying me."
"Everyone?"
"Everyone. Priya won't stop talking."
"Hm. When did you last drink water?"
"At lunch? Maybe."
"It's four o'clock and baking out here. Sit in the shade. Drink half this bottle, slowly."
"I'm fine."
"You're thirsty. Drink."
Five minutes later:
"Sir, my head's better. Sorry for snapping."
"Not your fault. New rule, whole team: water break every fifteen minutes."

qa.q: What time is it when Chetan asks about water?
qa.a: Four o'clock.

qa.q: What made Chetan suspect thirst rather than laziness?
qa.a: He was puzzled and concerned that Neelam, usually full of fire, was dragging her feet and complaining of a headache, so he asked about water.

qa.q: Why is Chetan's new rule wiser than pushing Neelam harder?
qa.a: Regular water breaks prevent the slump for the whole team, while pushing would only make a thirsty player slower and sharper.

qa.q: What was practice like for Neelam before the break?
qa.a: She had a headache and felt everyone was annoying, dropping passes even though she was trying.

grounding: Shows a coach noticing a keen teen turn slow and sharp in the heat without water, and water breaks changing her mood more than a pep talk.

subtype: Sports practice fatigue and short temper [Observer]
passage: I've coached under-16 football in Margao for six years, and I still think about one afternoon with Naveen. He was my most excited player, the kind who arrives early and begs for extra shooting practice. That day, in the April heat, he trailed behind in every drill, kicked a cone away when I corrected him, and told a younger boy to stop following him around. I nearly benched him for attitude. Then I saw him leaning on the goalpost, eyes half shut, lips dry. He had forgotten his bottle and was too proud to ask to borrow one. I sat him in the shade with water and a wet towel and called a break for everyone. Twenty minutes later he was laughing again. I'm Farida, and my first question to a grumpy player now is, "Have you had water?"

qa.q: What had Naveen forgotten?
qa.a: His bottle.

qa.q: How did Farida feel before spotting the dry lips, and what changed?
qa.a: Farida felt annoyed enough to bench him for attitude, then grew concerned on seeing him leaning on the goalpost with his eyes half shut and lips dry.

qa.q: What does Farida's first question to a grumpy player show?
qa.a: That checking for water and rest comes before blaming attitude, because a body need often explains the mood.

qa.q: Why might Naveen not have asked to borrow a bottle?
qa.a: He was too proud to ask, perhaps embarrassed to admit he had forgotten it.

grounding: Shows a coach noticing an eager teen become slow and sharp in the heat without water, and rest and water changing the mood more than a lecture.

passage:
Coach's log, under-16 girls' hockey, Thursday
Swati is normally first on the field, cheering everyone. Today, after ninety minutes of drills in the afternoon sun, she was dragging her stick, missing easy passes, and she snapped at her captain, 'Just leave me alone!' My first instinct was a pep talk to the whole team about attitude. Then I realised nobody had taken a water break since the warm-up, and her bottle sat still full on the bench. I stopped practice and sent everyone into the shade to drink and rest for ten minutes. When we restarted, Swati was calling for the ball again. From now on: water breaks every twenty minutes in the heat.
Zubin

qa.q: Where was Swati's bottle?
qa.a: Still full on the bench.

qa.q: What was Zubin's first instinct, and what did Zubin feel on noticing the full bottle?
qa.a: Zubin's first instinct was a pep talk about attitude, then Zubin felt concerned on seeing no one had had a water break.

qa.q: What rule did Zubin make?
qa.a: Water breaks every twenty minutes in the heat.

qa.q: What was practice like for Swati before the break?
qa.a: She was probably exhausted and irritable from heat and thirst, so every pass and word felt like too much.

grounding: A coach sees a keen teenager turn slow and sharp after training in heat without water and uses water breaks, not a pep talk.
